title: A letter to Newport (1790)
hook: to the Newport congregation, the government gives "to bigotry no sanction"

segments.voice: Yesterday, New Amsterdam, and your line: twenty-three arrived. Did someone new cross your path, and did you make a little room? Today, a later chapter in the same young country, told in two letters. Day nine hundred ninety.

A small congregation in Newport, Rhode Island, hears that the president of the new United States is coming to town. Their warden, Moses Seixas, sits down to write a welcome on their behalf. He chooses his words with care. Jews had lived under rulers who allowed them in one year and turned on them the next, so he writes about what kind of government this new one is. The president writes back. And when the reply arrives, Seixas's own phrase is in it. Today, that letter.
screen: `A WELCOME FROM NEWPORT.` → `A WARDEN CHOOSES HIS WORDS.` → `THE PRESIDENT WRITES BACK.`

segments.voice: Seixas described the new government as one that gives no approval to bigotry and no help to persecution. In the reply, the president took that phrase and gave it back as a promise: "For happily the Government of the United States, which gives to bigotry no sanction, to persecution no assistance, requires only that they who live under its protection should demean themselves as good citizens." Notice what happened. The line people quote from this letter was first written by a Jewish warden in Newport. The president heard it, and signed his name under it. Then the letter goes a step further. It says the time is past when people speak of toleration, as if one group's rights were a favor granted by another. Toleration means, we put up with you. The letter says something else: these rights belong to you already. They aren't a gift. And then, near the end, the letter reaches for the Hebrew prophets. It hopes that the children of Abraham in this land will keep the good will of their neighbors, while everyone sits in safety under his own vine and fig tree, with none to make him afraid. That's the prophet Micah's picture of peace. "And none shall make them afraid." A Jewish congregation's welcome, a phrase handed back, and a verse from Micah: the letter is all three. It didn't end bigotry. Jews in America would still meet plenty of it. But it gave them a sentence, from the top of the government, to hold the country to.
screen: `A WELCOME FROM NEWPORT.` · `THE PHRASE COMES BACK.` · `NOT TOLERATION: RIGHTS.` · `UNDER HIS OWN VINE AND FIG TREE.` · then, large: `TO BIGOTRY NO SANCTION.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: a thank-you for a freedom. Sit comfortably and let your breath settle. Think of one freedom you used today without noticing it: to pray or not pray, to speak your mind, to walk where you like, to read what you want. Hold it for a few breaths. Then ask whose work, courage or care keeps it in place: a teacher, a parent, a neighbor, someone who served, someone who wrote a law. Let one name come. Today, thank them, in a word, a note, or, if you pray, in prayer. The bell holds the time.
The letter to Newport. A president's reply to a Jewish congregation, promising a government that gives bigotry no sanction. Today's word.
Your line: no sanction to bigotry. Today, if you hear a cheap shot at someone's faith or people, don't give it your nod, not even a laugh. Day nine hundred ninety.

howItsDone: In Newport the president's letter is read aloud at a yearly public gathering at the old synagogue, and its phrase about bigotry is quoted when people speak about religious freedom in the United States.
